title: Trees: Validate a Binary Search Tree
oneLiner: Pass an allowed (low, high) range down the tree; every node must fall strictly inside the range its ancestors set.
keyTakeaway: A BST rule is about whole subtrees, not just parent and child: everything in the left subtree must be smaller than the node, everything in the right subtree larger. Carry that as bounds: going left, the node's value becomes the new HIGH; going right, it becomes the new LOW. One DFS, O(n).
explanation:
You get the root of a binary tree, built from a level-order array where null marks a missing child (so [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7] means 5 has children 4 and 6, 4 has none, and 6 has children 3 and 7). Return true if it is a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly smaller and all values in its right subtree are strictly larger. Duplicates make it invalid.

The tempting answer checks each node against its two children: left.val < node.val < right.val. That is not enough. In [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7] every parent-child pair looks fine (3 < 6 < 7), yet 3 sits in the right subtree of 5, so the tree is broken. A local check can't see a rule that an ancestor two levels up imposes.

The fix is to pass that information down. Each call gets the range (low, high) its value must sit in. The root may be anything: (-∞, +∞). When you step into a left child, the current node's value becomes the upper bound; into a right child, it becomes the lower bound; the other bound is inherited unchanged. So 6 is checked against (5, +∞), and its left child 3 against (5, 6) -- and fails. A null child is trivially valid. Every node is visited once: O(n) time, O(h) stack space.

Two equally good alternatives come up in interviews. An inorder traversal of a BST visits values in strictly increasing order, so you can walk inorder and check that each value beats the previous one. And follow-ups often ask about the sentinel: if values can be as small as the minimum int, using int.MinValue as "no lower bound" wrongly rejects a node equal to it. Use a wider type (long), or a null meaning "no bound".

visualizationSteps.message: Every parent-child pair here looks fine (4 < 5 < 6 and 3 < 6 < 7). Check it properly: carry an allowed (low, high) range down from the root.
Root 5 has no limits: range (-∞, +∞). OK. Its left subtree must stay below 5, its right subtree above 5.
Node 4 must be inside (-∞, 5). It is. Going left, 4 becomes the new high; going right, it becomes the new low.
Node 6 must be inside (5, +∞). It is. Going left, 6 becomes the new high; going right, it becomes the new low.
Node 3 must be inside (5, 6), but 3 <= 5. It sits in the right subtree of 5, so it must be larger. Invalid: return false all the way up.
Result: false. Comparing 3 only with its parent 6 would have missed this -- the bound 5 came from two levels up.

pythonHarnessPreamble:
null = None

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def build_level_order_tree(values):
    # Builds a tree from a LeetCode-style level-order list; null (None) marks a missing child.
    if not values or values[0] is None:
        return None
    root = TreeNode(values[0])
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    i = 1
    while head < len(queue) and i < len(values):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if values[i] is not None:
            node.left = TreeNode(values[i])
            queue.append(node.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(values) and values[i] is not None:
            node.right = TreeNode(values[i])
            queue.append(node.right)
        i += 1
    return root
recognitionSignals: "Is this a valid BST?" or any rule that must hold for a node against ALL of its ancestors, not just its parent.
Information flows top-down: what a node is allowed to be depends on the path from the root to it.
The problem mentions sorted order in a tree, which is a hint that an inorder walk or range bounds will help.
gotchas: Comparing a node only with its direct children passes trees like [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7], where 3 is below 6 but still inside 5's right subtree.
Using int.MinValue / int.MaxValue as "no bound" breaks when a node actually holds that value. Use long bounds or null.
Use strict comparisons: a value equal to a bound (a duplicate) makes the tree invalid here.
confusableWith: Binary Trees: Inorder Traversal (DFS) visits nodes in sorted order for a BST; checking that the inorder sequence strictly increases is a valid second solution to this same problem.
Binary Search Trees: Search walks ONE root-to-leaf path because it trusts the BST rule; validating has to visit every node because it is checking that rule.

complexity.note: Every node is checked once against its (low, high) range; the recursion is as deep as the tree is tall -- O(log n) balanced, O(n) for a skewed tree.
